summary: This document defines a URN namespace identifier for generating URNs suitable for use in documentation and in testing or experimenting with URN-related technology.

plainLanguage.summary: When writing examples you need pretend names that will never clash with real ones. This sets aside a safe set of pretend names.

questions: how to write example urns in documentation
what is a urn namespace identifier
subtitle: A reserved URN namespace, urn:example, for safe pretend identifiers in documentation and tests.

tldr.problem: Writers of documentation and tests need made-up URNs that will never clash with real ones, but experimental X-NID namespaces had fallen out of favor and fake unregistered NIDs cause confusion.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6963 registers a formal URN namespace identifier, example, so anyone can mint URNs of the form urn:example:{NSS} by choosing their own Namespace Specific String.
tldr.outcome: Authors get a clean, recognizable place for example URNs. They are not meant to be resolved, and they should not be used for anything beyond documentation, private testing and experiments.

today: RFC 6963 is a Best Current Practice published in May 2013, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The example NID is registered in the "Formal URN Namespaces" registry according to its IANA section.

sections.title: Why an Example Namespace
sections.content:
A Uniform Resource Name (URN) is a persistent, location-independent identifier, and its scope comes from its namespace identifier (NID). RFC 3406 defines three kinds of NIDs: formal, informal and experimental. Experimental NIDs take the form X-NID, but the "X-" convention has been deprecated in general (RFC 6648).

So this document registers a formal NID, example, in the same spirit as example.com and other reserved domain names (RFC 2606). Under it, authors and developers can mint URNs for documentation, testing of URN and URI processing, experimentation and invalid URNs, with no fear of conflicts with current or future real URNs.

These URNs are not meant for testing non-URI code or building higher-level applications such as XML namespace names, since it is easy to mint a URI whose authority is a domain name you control.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of inventing silly made-up address labels that might accidentally match a real one, everyone can use one official "pretend" label.

sections.title: The Registered Namespace
sections.content:
The completed registration template (Version 1, dated 2013-04-24) names the IETF as registering organization, with the IESG as designated contact. URNs have this structure:

urn:example:{NSS}

The Namespace Specific String (NSS) is a mandatory string of ASCII characters that follows the URN syntax of RFC 2141 and gives a name that is useful within the relevant example, test suite or other application. Lexical equivalence follows RFC 2141, and there is no validation mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: Every pretend name starts with urn:example: and then you add whatever name you like to finish it.

sections.title: Assignment, Uniqueness and Resolution
sections.content:
Assignment is completely open: anyone can mint example URNs. Minters ought to strive for unique NSS values, but uniqueness cannot be guaranteed by the assignment process. Because of that, it is NOT RECOMMENDED to use example URNs for anything other than documentation, private testing and truly experimental contexts.

Once minted, an example URN is immutable, although nothing guarantees that the documentation or test using it stays unchanged. Example URNs are not intended to be resolved, and the namespace will probably never be registered with a Resolution Discovery System, except to tell requesters that these are merely examples. The scope of an example URN is limited to the documentation, test or experiment in which it appears; it has no meaning outside that.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone can make up a pretend name, and since nobody hands them out, two people might pick the same one. That is fine for practice, but you should not use them for real things.

sections.title: Namespace and Community Considerations
sections.content:
No existing formal namespace is meant for example URNs. Experimental namespaces could be minted at will, but they conflict with the move away from "X-" names, and in practice authors often use fake NIDs that never get registered. A dedicated example namespace is recommended to reduce confusion.

It does not remove the need to work with the right authorities. The RFC gives three cases: use urn:example:xmpp:foo rather than requesting urn:xmpp:foo, register a new NID if existing ones do not fit your function (rather than, say, urn:example:sha-1:... in place of the sha-1 NID), and do not set up shadow NIDs like urn:example:MyCompany:* instead of using, for instance, HTTP URIs. There is no issuing authority for example URNs.
sections.plainLanguage: The pretend names are for practice pages only. If you really need a real name in a real system, you still have to ask the people who run that system.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content: The document introduces no additional security considerations beyond those of URN use and resolution in general. For IANA, it defines the registration of the example NID, which IANA has added to the "Formal URN Namespaces" registry.
sections.plainLanguage: Pretend names add no new dangers, and the official list of namespaces now includes this one.
